library(lmtest)

::: {.callout-note}
## How to use this

- This is **not** the real exam. Nobody has seen that yet. The tasks follow the lab exercises (Labs 2–5) with variables the labs didn't use.
- Set a timer for 90 minutes. Work in your own project, in a script named `Lastname_Firstname_mock.R`.
- Write a `# Interpretation:` comment in your own words after every result.
- Then open the solutions and compare. The numbers should match, your sentences don't need to.
:::

## The data

The European Social Survey, round 11 (`ess.csv` from the labs). Each row is one respondent.

| Variable | Question | Codes |
|---|---|---|
| `stfdem` | How satisfied with the way democracy works in your country? | 0 = extremely dissatisfied … 10 = extremely satisfied, 77, 88, 99 = missing |
| `vote` | Voted in the last national election? | 1 = yes, 2 = no, 3 = not eligible to vote, 7, 8, 9 = missing |
| `polintr` | How interested in politics? | 1 = very, 2 = quite, 3 = hardly, 4 = not at all interested, 7, 8, 9 = missing |
| `agea` | Age | 999 = missing |
| `gndr` | Gender | 1 = male, 2 = female |
| `eduyrs` | Years of full-time education | 77, 88, 99 = missing |
| `cntry` | Country | two-letter code |

## Tasks

1. **Clean** `stfdem` into `swd` (0–10), `vote` into `voted` (1 = voted, 0 = didn't vote, not eligible and the missing codes become `NA`), and `polintr` into `interested` (1 = very or quite interested, 0 = hardly or not at all). Also clean `agea` and `eduyrs`. Check every new variable.
2. **Describe** `swd`: mean, median, standard deviation and a histogram. What percentage of respondents voted?
3. Is political interest **associated** with voting? Give the percentages and the test.
4. Is satisfaction with democracy **different** for voters and non-voters?
5. What is the **correlation** between satisfaction with democracy and years of education?
6. Estimate an **OLS regression** of `swd` on age, gender, education, `interested` and country fixed effects. Interpret the coefficients and the R².
7. Test the OLS model for **heteroskedasticity** and **multicollinearity**.
8. Estimate a **logistic regression** of `voted` on `swd`, age, gender, education and country fixed effects. Calculate the **marginal effects** and interpret the one for `swd`.
9. Does the effect of education on `swd` **depend on** political interest? Estimate the OLS model from task 6 with an interaction between education and `interested`.

## Solutions

Open them only after you've tried.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 1 · Clean

```{r}
dataset <- read.csv("data/ess_lab.csv")   # in your project: read.csv("data/ess.csv")

table(dataset$stfdem, useNA = "ifany")
dataset$swd <- ifelse(dataset$stfdem >= 0 & dataset$stfdem <= 10, dataset$stfdem, NA)
table(dataset$swd, useNA = "ifany")

table(dataset$vote, useNA = "ifany")
dataset$voted <- ifelse(dataset$vote == 1, 1, ifelse(dataset$vote == 2, 0, NA))
table(dataset$vote, dataset$voted, useNA = "ifany")

table(dataset$polintr, useNA = "ifany")
dataset$interested <- ifelse(dataset$polintr %in% c(1, 2), 1,
                             ifelse(dataset$polintr %in% c(3, 4), 0, NA))
table(dataset$polintr, dataset$interested, useNA = "ifany")

dataset$age <- ifelse(dataset$agea == 999, NA, dataset$agea)
dataset$edu <- ifelse(dataset$eduyrs %in% c(77, 88, 99), NA, dataset$eduyrs)
summary(dataset$age)
summary(dataset$edu)
```

**The traps:**

- `vote = 3` ("not eligible") is not "didn't vote", so it becomes `NA`.
- `polintr` runs backwards: **1** is the *most* interested.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 2 · Describe

```{r}
mean(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE)
median(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE)
hist(dataset$swd, breaks = seq(-0.5, 10.5, by = 1),
     main = "Satisfaction with democracy", xlab = "0 = extremely dissatisfied, 10 = extremely satisfied")
round(prop.table(table(dataset$voted)) * 100, 1)
```

> Mean: `r round(mean(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`. Median: `r median(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE)`. Standard deviation: `r round(sd(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`.
>
> Given that the mean and the median are very close, the distribution of satisfaction with democracy is approximately symmetric, around the middle of the 0-10 scale. The standard deviation means that values typically lie about `r round(sd(dataset$swd, na.rm = TRUE), 1)` points from the mean, about half of the mean, so the spread of the distribution is fairly large.
>
> `r round(100 * mean(dataset$voted, na.rm = TRUE), 1)`% of the eligible respondents who answered say they voted in the last national election.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 3 · Interest and voting (chi-square)

```{r}
tab <- table(dataset$interested, dataset$voted)   # rows: interested, columns: voted
tab
round(prop.table(tab, margin = 1) * 100, 1)       # % who voted within each interest group
chisq.test(tab)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
chi <- chisq.test(tab)
pc <- round(prop.table(tab, margin = 1) * 100)
```

> X² = `r round(chi$statistic, 1)` (df = `r chi$parameter`, `r p_txt(chi$p.value)`). The association is `r sig_txt(chi$p.value)`, so we reject the null hypothesis of no association between political interest and voting. The chi-square test gives no direction, but the percentages do: `r pc["1", "1"]`% of the interested voted, against `r pc["0", "1"]`% of the uninterested.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 4 · Satisfaction by vote (t-test)

```{r}
t.test(swd ~ voted, data = dataset)
boxplot(swd ~ voted, data = dataset, names = c("Didn't vote", "Voted"),
        ylab = "Satisfaction with democracy (0-10)")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
tt <- t.test(swd ~ voted, data = dataset)
```

> Non-voters have a mean satisfaction of `r round(tt$estimate[1], 2)` and voters `r round(tt$estimate[2], 2)` (t = `r round(tt$statistic, 2)`, `r p_txt(tt$p.value)`). The difference is `r sig_txt(tt$p.value)`, so we reject the null hypothesis that the means are not different: voters are more satisfied with democracy. The scale runs the "normal" way (higher = more satisfied), unlike Lab 3's satisfaction variable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 5 · Correlation

```{r}
cor(dataset$swd, dataset$edu, use = "complete.obs")
cor.test(dataset$swd, dataset$edu)
```

```{r}
#| include: false
ct <- cor.test(dataset$swd, dataset$edu)
```

> Correlation: `r round(ct$estimate, 2)`. There is a `r r_dir(ct$estimate)`, `r r_label(ct$estimate)` association between satisfaction with democracy and education, so that the more educated someone is, the very slightly more satisfied with democracy they are. It is `r sig_txt(ct$p.value)` because the sample is large, but a statistically significant association is not always a strong one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 6 · OLS regression

```{r}
model1 <- lm(swd ~ age + factor(gndr) + edu + interested + factor(cntry), data = dataset)
summary(model1)$coefficients[1:5, ]    # summary(model1) shows the full output
summary(model1)$r.squared
nobs(model1)
```

> Net of the other variables and the country fixed effects:
>
> - When age increases by one year, satisfaction with democracy decreases by `r abs(b(model1, "age", 4))` points (`r sig(model1, "age")`), so about `r abs(round(10 * coef(model1)[["age"]], 2))` points per decade: statistically significant, but small.
> - Satisfaction is `r abs(b(model1, "factor(gndr)2"))` points `r if (coef(model1)[["factor(gndr)2"]] > 0) "higher" else "lower"` for women than for men, the reference category, but this is `r sig(model1, "factor(gndr)2")` (`r p(model1, "factor(gndr)2")`): we cannot reject the null hypothesis of no effect of gender.
> - When education increases by one year, satisfaction increases by `r b(model1, "edu")` points (`r sig(model1, "edu")`).
> - Satisfaction is `r b(model1, "interested", 2)` points higher for people interested in politics than for the uninterested (`r sig(model1, "interested")`), the largest effect in the model.
>
> R² = `r round(summary(model1)$r.squared, 3)`: the independent variables, including the country fixed effects, explain `r round(100 * summary(model1)$r.squared, 1)`% of the variance of satisfaction with democracy (N = `r format(nobs(model1), big.mark = ",")`).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 7 · Diagnostics

```{r}
plot(model1$fitted.values, model1$residuals, xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")
bptest(model1)
vif(model1)
```

> The Breusch-Pagan test rejects homoskedasticity (BP = `r round(bptest(model1)$statistic)`, `r p_txt(bptest(model1)$p.value)`), so there is heteroskedasticity: the variance of the residuals is not the same across the values of the dependent variable. The quick fix is to use robust standard errors. All the VIFs are close to 1 (largest `r round(max(vif(model1)[, 1]), 2)`), well below 10, so multicollinearity is not a concern.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 8 · Logistic regression and marginal effects

```{r}
logit1 <- glm(voted ~ swd + age + factor(gndr) + edu + factor(cntry),
              data = dataset, family = binomial)
summary(logit1)$coefficients[1:5, ]
summary(margins(logit1, variables = c("swd", "age", "gndr", "edu")))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
me <- summary(margins(logit1, variables = c("swd", "age", "gndr", "edu")))
ame <- setNames(me$AME, me$factor)
mep <- setNames(me$p, me$factor)
```

> The coefficient of `swd` is positive, so more satisfied people are more likely to have voted (logit coefficients cannot be interpreted beyond their sign). The marginal effect is `r round(ame[["swd"]], 3)`: when satisfaction with democracy increases by one point, the probability of having voted increases by `r round(100 * ame[["swd"]], 1)` percentage points (`r sig_txt(mep[["swd"]])`), net of age, gender, education and the country fixed effects. When education increases by one year, it increases by `r round(100 * ame[["edu"]], 1)` percentage points.
>
> This shows an association, not a cause: voting may also make people more satisfied.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 9 · Interaction

```{r}
model_int <- lm(swd ~ age + factor(gndr) + edu * interested + factor(cntry), data = dataset)
summary(model_int)$coefficients[c("edu", "interested", "edu:interested"), ]
coef(model_int)[["edu"]] + coef(model_int)[["edu:interested"]]   # education slope for the interested
```

> For the uninterested (the reference, `interested` = 0), each year of education raises satisfaction by `r b(model_int, "edu")` points. For the interested, by `r b(model_int, "edu")` + `r b(model_int, "edu:interested")` = `r round(coef(model_int)[["edu"]] + coef(model_int)[["edu:interested"]], 3)` points. The interaction is `r sig(model_int, "edu:interested")` (`r p(model_int, "edu:interested")`) but not at the 0.05 level, so the evidence that political interest moderates the effect of education is weak.
:::
